title: RNN, LSTM & Sequence Models
summary: The pre-transformer sequence toolkit — RNN, LSTM, and GRU — and why attention eventually replaced them for most sequence tasks.

slides.markdown:
Ordinary feedforward networks have no memory — each input is processed in isolation. **Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs)** fix that by carrying a **hidden state** forward from one step of a sequence to the next, giving the network a working memory of what it's seen so far.

RNNs and their better-behaved descendants, **LSTM** and **GRU**, were the standard tool for text, speech, and time-series before attention-based Transformers took over most of that territory.

slides.subTitle: Shared weights, a hidden state as memory
slides.markdown:
At each step, an RNN takes the current input **and** its own previous hidden state, and produces a new hidden state (plus optionally an output) — using the **same weights** at every time step.

That hidden state is the network's memory: it's a compressed summary of everything the sequence has shown it so far, updated as new inputs arrive. Because the weights are shared across time steps, the network can process sequences of any length with a fixed number of parameters.

slides.subTitle: Unrolled through time
slides.markdown:
"Unrolling" an RNN makes its recurrence visible as a chain — the same cell repeated once per time step, passing its hidden state forward.

![An RNN unrolled through time](assets/rnn-unrolled.svg)

Each copy in the chain shares identical weights; only the hidden state and the current input change from step to step. Backpropagation through this unrolled chain is called **backpropagation through time (BPTT)**.

slides.subTitle: Why vanilla RNNs forget
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "An RNN's hidden state means it can remember information from arbitrarily far back in a sequence."

**Why it's wrong:** BPTT multiplies gradients across every time step going backward, exactly like depth does in a very deep feedforward network. Over long sequences (hundreds of steps), those repeated multiplications **vanish** toward zero (or occasionally **explode**) — so the gradient signal from an early time step barely reaches the weights by the time it's needed, and the network effectively can't learn long-range dependencies.

**Correct model:** vanilla RNNs reliably capture only **short-range** dependencies; anything requiring memory across dozens or hundreds of steps needs a gating mechanism like LSTM or GRU, or an attention-based model instead.

slides.subTitle: Gates as a fix for long-range memory
slides.markdown:
An **LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory)** cell adds a separate **cell state** — a memory highway that information can travel along largely unchanged — plus three learned **gates** that control it:

- **Forget gate** — decides what to discard from the cell state.
- **Input gate** — decides what new information to add.
- **Output gate** — decides what part of the cell state to expose as the hidden state.

Because the cell state's update is closer to addition than repeated multiplication, gradients can flow across many more time steps without vanishing — the specific fix for vanilla RNNs' core weakness.

slides.subTitle: A simpler alternative to LSTM
slides.markdown:
A **GRU (Gated Recurrent Unit)** achieves a similar effect to LSTM with fewer moving parts: it merges the cell state and hidden state into one, and combines the three LSTM gates into two — an **update gate** and a **reset gate**.

Fewer parameters mean faster training and less data needed to fit them, at the cost of slightly less expressive control over memory than LSTM's three separate gates. In practice, the two often perform comparably, and the choice frequently comes down to compute budget.

slides.subTitle: Capacity vs compute cost
slides.markdown:
| | RNN | LSTM | GRU |
|---|---|---|---|
| Long-range memory | Poor | Strong | Strong |
| Parameters per cell | Fewest | Most (3 gates) | Fewer (2 gates) |
| Training speed | Fastest | Slowest | Faster than LSTM |
| Default choice today | Rarely used alone | Common baseline | Common when compute-constrained |

**How to decide:** default to LSTM or GRU over a vanilla RNN whenever the sequence has any meaningful long-range structure; pick GRU over LSTM when you want comparable results with less compute and less data.

slides.subTitle: Attention and Transformers
slides.markdown:
RNNs (and LSTM/GRU) process a sequence **one step at a time**, so training can't be parallelized across time steps, and even gated memory degrades over very long sequences.

**Attention** (see [Attention & Transformer Architecture](attention-transformer-architecture)) lets a model look directly at any position in the sequence in a single step, with no recurrence at all — enabling full parallelization during training and much stronger long-range dependency modeling. That combination is why Transformers displaced RNN-based models for most sequence tasks, from translation to language modeling.

slides.subTitle: Bidirectional RNNs
slides.markdown:
A standard RNN's hidden state at step `t` only reflects what came **before** `t` — fine for generation (the future genuinely doesn't exist yet), but limiting for tasks where the whole sequence is available upfront, like tagging each word in a sentence with its part of speech.

A **bidirectional RNN** runs two separate RNNs over the sequence — one left-to-right, one right-to-left — and concatenates their hidden states at each position, so every step's representation is informed by context on both sides. This is standard for classification and tagging tasks (sentiment analysis, named entity recognition) but doesn't apply to autoregressive generation, where future tokens genuinely aren't available yet at inference time.
